title: Simultaneous prime-to-ell field sections over separable charts
statement: Let $K$ be a field, let $\ell$ be a prime different from the characteristic of $K$, and let $I$ be a finite set. For each $i\in I$ let $K_i/K$ be a finite separable field extension [def-pc-field-extension, def-weil-pbc-separable-algebraic-extension], and let $F_i/K_i$ be a finite field extension whose degree is prime to $\ell$. There exists a finite field extension $K'/K$ of degree prime to $\ell$ such that, for every $i$ and every field factor $M$ of the finite etale $K'$-algebra $K_i\otimes_K K'$ [def-weil-pbc-module-tensor-product], with multiplication $(a\otimes b)(c\otimes d)=ac\otimes bd$, there is a $K_i$-algebra homomorphism $F_i\to M$. A field factor here means a quotient by a maximal ideal, equipped with the maps induced by $K_i\to K_i\otimes_K K'$ and $K'\to K_i\otimes_K K'$. Degrees mean dimensions as vector spaces [def-weil-vector-space-dimension]. The extension $F_i/K_i$ need not be separable, and $I$ may be empty.

source.place: Expose II, proof of Theorem 3.2.1, quasi-Galois extension L/K, Sylow fixed field and the descent argument using Proposition 2.2.6, printed pp. 29--30. This isolates only its simultaneous field-factor assertion, allowing inseparable degrees prime to ell.

proof.text: If $I=\varnothing$, take $K\prime=K$; its degree is $1$ and the remaining quantifiers are empty. Henceforth suppose $I$ is nonempty. Each $F_i/K$ is finite by degree multiplicativity for $K\subseteq K_i\subseteq F_i$. In particular it is algebraic: powers of any element are linearly dependent in its finite-dimensional $K$-vector space. Choose an algebraic closure $\Omega_0/K$ and, by the algebraic-embedding lemma, choose $K$-embeddings $F_i\to\Omega_0$. Restrict these embeddings to $K_i$ so that the two maps in each tower remain compatible.

source.place: Tags 09G9 (lemma-multiplicativity-degrees), 09GT (algebraic closure existence), 09GU (lemma-map-into-algebraic-closure); ILO II 3.2.1, printed p. 29, compositum preparation.

proof.text: Choose a $K$-basis $\mathcal B_i$ of each image of $F_i$ in $\Omega_0$. Let $E$ be the $K$-span in $\Omega_0$ of the finite family of products $\prod_{i\in I}b_i$ with $b_i\in\mathcal B_i$. Expanding $1$ in each basis shows that $1$ and every image $F_i$ lie in $E$. Expanding each product $b_ic_i$ in $\mathcal B_i$ shows that $E$ is closed under multiplication. Thus $E$ is a finite-dimensional commutative $K$-algebra and a domain, since it is a subring of a field. The finite-dimensional-domain lemma makes it a field. Apply the normal-closure lemma to $E/K$ to obtain a finite normal extension $L/K$ containing these compatible copies of all $F_i$ and $K_i$. Choose an algebraic closure $\Omega$ of $L$, and identify all these fields with their images in it.

source.place: Tag 09DT (lemma-normal-closure); finite compositum used in ILO II 3.2.1, printed p. 29. The finite-span construction preceding normal closure is written out.

proof.text: Let $G=\operatorname{Aut}_K(L)$. It is finite, since it is a subset of the finite set of $K$-embeddings $L\to L$. Choose an $\ell$-Sylow subgroup $P\subseteq G$: write $|P|=\ell^a$ and $d=[G:P]$, with $\ell\nmid d$. Define $K\prime=L^P=\{x\in L:\sigma(x)=x\text{ for all }\sigma\in P\}$. This is a subfield containing $K$ (the fixed-element equations are preserved by addition, multiplication and inverse), finite-dimensional over $K$ as a $K$-subspace of $L$. The action of $P$ on $L$ is faithful because $P$ is a subgroup of its automorphism group. The finite faithful action theorem therefore gives $[L:K\prime]=|P|=\ell^a$.

source.place: Expose II, proof of Theorem 3.2.1, printed p. 30, Sylow subgroup and fixed field; Stacks Tag 09I3 (lemma-galois-over-fixed-field).

proof.text: In characteristic $p>0$, apply the normal-degree-factor theorem to the finite normal extension $L/K$ and the algebraic closure $\Omega$ chosen above. It gives $[L:K]=|G|p^c$ for some $c\geq0$. Cosets partition the finite group $G$ into $d$ sets each of size $|P|$, so $|G|=d|P|$. Degree multiplicativity in $K\subseteq K\prime\subseteq L$ and $[L:K\prime]=|P|$ give $|P|[K\prime:K]=d|P|p^c$, hence $[K\prime:K]=dp^c$. Both $d$ and $p$ are prime to $\ell$, by the Sylow choice and the hypothesis $\ell\ne p$, respectively. Thus this degree is prime to $\ell$.

source.place: Expose II, proof of Theorem 3.2.1, printed p. 30, degree of the Sylow fixed field; Stacks Tags 09HS, 09HJ, 030L, 09HI and 09G9 as in the cited degree nodes.

proof.text: In characteristic $0$, put $S=L^G$. Since $L/K$ is algebraic normal, the fixed-field purely-inseparable theorem gives $S/K$ purely inseparable; by the characteristic-zero clause of that definition this says $S=K$. Apply the faithful finite action theorem to $G$ acting on $L$. It gives $[L:K]=[L:S]=|G|$. As in the preceding step, $|G|=d|P|$ and degree multiplicativity cancel $|P|=[L:K\prime]$ to give $[K\prime:K]=d$, again prime to $\ell$. This completes the degree assertion in every characteristic.

source.place: Expose II, proof of Theorem 3.2.1, printed p. 30; Stacks Tags 030M (lemma-normal-case), 09I3 and 09G9. Characteristic zero is made explicit using the cited definition.

proof.text: Fix $i$ and any maximal-ideal quotient $q:K_i\otimes_KK\prime\twoheadrightarrow M$ in the statement. The images of $e_j\otimes1$, for a $K$-basis $(e_j)$ of $K_i$, span $M$ over $K\prime$: every tensor is a finite sum of pure tensors. Hence $M/K\prime$ is finite and algebraic. Extend $K\prime\hookrightarrow\Omega$ to an embedding $u:M\hookrightarrow\Omega$ by the algebraic-embedding lemma. For $x\in K_i$, its minimal polynomial over $K$ splits in $L$ because the copy $K_i\subset L$ of step 2 lies in the normal extension $L/K$. The element $u(q(x\otimes1))$ is another root of that same polynomial, so belongs to $L$: in the field $\Omega$, a product of linear factors vanishes only if one factor vanishes. Also $u(q(1\otimes b))=b\in K\prime$ for $b\in K\prime$. Surjectivity of $q$ and the finite-sum tensor description now imply $u(M)\subseteq L$. Identify $M$ with this subfield of $L$; this retains its actual $K_i$-map, which may differ from the initial copy of $K_i$ in $L$.

source.place: Expose II, proof of Theorem 3.2.1, printed pp. 29--30, generic components after the normal extension; Stacks Tag 09GU. Root containment is the definition of normality from step 2, with its polynomial argument written out.

proof.text: The finite $K\prime$-spanning set of $L$ is also an $M$-spanning set, so $L/M$ is finite. Degree multiplicativity gives $\ell^a=[L:K\prime]=[L:M][M:K\prime]$. Thus $[L:M]$ divides $\ell^a$. With the actual map $K_i\to M$ fixed in step 6, form the commutative $M$-algebra $B=M\otimes_{K_i}F_i$, with the tensor multiplication and unit. Scalar-extension dimension gives $\dim_M B=[F_i:K_i]=n_i$, where $\ell\nmid n_i$. In particular $B\ne0$. Every strict chain of $B$-submodules of its regular module is a strict chain of $M$-subspaces, so has length at most $n_i$ (dimension rises by at least one per inclusion). The definition of module length therefore gives finite length of $B$ as a $B$-module. Apply the simple-filtration theorem to obtain $0=B_0\subsetneq\cdots\subsetneq B_r=B$ with simple $B$-module quotients $Q_j=B_j/B_{j-1}$.

source.place: Tags 02LY (definition-length) and 00J3 (lemma-simple-pieces); field degree/base-change nodes supply the displayed dimensions. This expands ILO II 3.2.1, p. 30, choice of a generic point of degree prime to ell.

proof.text: For each simple quotient $Q_j$, choose $0\ne v_j\in Q_j$. The image of $B\to Q_j$, $b\mapsto bv_j$, is a nonzero $B$-submodule, hence all of $Q_j$. Write $\mathfrak m_j$ for its kernel. The induced bijection $B/\mathfrak m_j\to Q_j$ is $M$-linear. The ideal $\mathfrak m_j$ is maximal: any ideal properly containing it has nonzero image in $Q_j$, hence image $Q_j$; choose $b$ in that ideal with $bv_j=v_j$, so $1-b\in\mathfrak m_j$ and the ideal contains $1$. Thus $N_j=B/\mathfrak m_j$ is a field and $[N_j:M]=\dim_M Q_j$. Extending a basis of $B_{j-1}$ to one of $B_j$ gives $\dim_M B_j=\dim_M B_{j-1}+\dim_M Q_j$; telescoping gives $n_i=\sum_{j=1}^r[N_j:M]$. If every summand were divisible by $\ell$, so would be $n_i$. Choose a $j$ for which $\ell\nmid[N_j:M]$, and put $N=N_j$. This argument retains multiplicities and works even when $B$ has nilpotents.

source.place: Tag 00J2 (lemma-characterize-length-1), cyclic-vector proof of simple modules as maximal-ideal quotients, written out here; Tag 00J3 (lemma-simple-pieces). Dimension additivity is shown by basis extension, not inferred from a definition node.

proof.text: The field $N/M$ is finite since it is a quotient of the finite-dimensional $M$-space $B$. Extend the inclusion $M\hookrightarrow\Omega$ of step 6 to an embedding $v:N\hookrightarrow\Omega$ by the algebraic-embedding lemma. The composite $F_i\to B\to N\xrightarrow{v}\Omega$ is a $K$-field embedding. For each $x\in F_i$, its image is a root of the minimal polynomial of $x$ over $K$. That polynomial splits in $L$, since the original copy $F_i\subset L$ belongs to the normal extension of step 2; the same linear-factor argument as in step 6 places this image in $L$. The image of $M$ is already contained in $L$. Every element of $N$ is the image of a finite sum of pure tensors from $B$, so $v(N)\subseteq L$. Thus, preserving the actual map from $M$, view $M\subseteq N\subseteq L$.

source.place: Expose II, proof of Theorem 3.2.1, printed p. 30, section over the quasi-Galois extension; Stacks Tag 09GU. This explicitly handles an inseparable F_i/K_i and its prescribed K_i-map.

proof.text: Degree multiplicativity in $M\subseteq N\subseteq L$ shows that $[N:M]$ divides $[L:M]$, hence divides $\ell^a$ by step 7. By step 8 it is also prime to $\ell$, so $[N:M]=1$. Therefore the structural inclusion $M\to N$ is an isomorphism: $1$ is a basis of the one-dimensional $M$-space $N$, so each element lies in $M$. Compose $F_i\to B\to N$ with its inverse $N\to M$. The tensor relation identifies the two maps from $K_i$ into $B$, and the inverse fixes $M$, so this is a homomorphism of $K_i$-algebras for the exact $K_i\to M$ map of the chosen quotient. Since $i$ and the maximal-ideal quotient $M$ were arbitrary, the same $K\prime$ gives every required section.
